title: Mini Exam Simulation
description: A practice run: a random task, preparation timer, speaking timer, examiner questions and self-evaluation.
intro: This is a PRACTICE simulation, not the official exam format. You get a random task, prepare with a timer, speak without interruption, then answer follow-up questions as if an examiner were asking them. Finally, you assess yourself. Ask your teacher about the exact format and timing of the oral exam at your school.

exercises.title: Switching off the news
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Background
stimulus.content: International surveys such as the Reuters Institute Digital News Report have found that many people say they sometimes or often avoid the news. Common reasons include feeling worn out by the amount of news, its negative effect on mood, and a feeling of powerlessness.

exercises.task: Give a talk about news avoidance.
content_points: explain why people might avoid the news
discuss the consequences for individuals and for democracy
suggest what media organisations could do differently
follow_up_questions: How do you personally keep up with the news?
Is it irresponsible to avoid the news completely?
What is “constructive” or “solutions-focused” journalism, and could it help?
Should schools encourage students to follow the news? How?
Does social media make the news feel more overwhelming?

model_outline.heading: Introduction
points: mention that surveys report it is widespread

model_outline.heading: Consequences
points: individuals: less informed, but possibly less stressed
democracy: uninformed voters, easier to manipulate

model_outline.heading: Solutions and conclusion
points: constructive journalism, explanatory formats, less sensationalism
balanced personal diet: informed but not overwhelmed

exercises.title: 87 unread messages
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: A teenager is lying in bed in a dark room late at night. The only light comes from a smartphone screen. The notification on the screen reads: “Class group: 87 unread messages”. On the bedside table there is an alarm clock showing 00:43 and an open textbook.

exercises.task: Give a talk about the pressure to be constantly available.
content_points: describe and interpret the picture
explain why people feel they must always be available
discuss effects on sleep, school and relationships
suggest ways to set healthy boundaries
follow_up_questions: Do you ever feel pressure to reply immediately? Why?
Should group chats have rules, for example no messages after 10 p.m.?
Some countries have discussed a “right to disconnect” for employees. Is this a good idea?
Is it rude not to reply to a message for a whole day?
How would you help a younger sibling who can’t put their phone down at night?

useful_phrases.label: Describing
phrases: The time on the clock suggests that …

useful_phrases.label: Giving advice
phrases: It would be a good idea to …

model_outline.heading: Describe and interpret
points: late at night, endless group chat, homework unfinished

model_outline.heading: Reasons
points: fear of missing out, social expectations, read receipts

model_outline.heading: Effects
points: stress and anxiety, but also feeling connected

model_outline.heading: Boundaries
points: phone out of the bedroom, do-not-disturb mode
conclusion: availability should be a choice

exercises.title: Unboxing for kids
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: A child of about six is sitting on a sofa holding a tablet. On the screen, a smiling young presenter is opening a large box of colourful toys. The child is staring at the screen excitedly. Next to the sofa there is a shopping bag from a toy shop.

exercises.task: Give a talk about advertising aimed at children online.
content_points: describe the picture
explain why online videos can be a powerful form of advertising for children
discuss who is responsible for protecting children
give your opinion on whether stricter rules are needed
follow_up_questions: At what age do you think children understand that something is an advert?
Should advertising to young children be banned completely?
What role should parents play?
Do you remember adverts that influenced you as a child?
Are there any positive sides to children’s content online?

model_outline.heading: Describe
points: young child, unboxing video, shopping bag – the video worked

model_outline.heading: Why it is powerful
points: children trust presenters, cannot recognise persuasive intent

model_outline.heading: Opinion
points: stricter rules for content aimed at young children
plus media education from an early age

exercises.title: Faces in the crowd
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: A busy train station. Several cameras are mounted on the ceiling. On a large monitor in a control room, the faces of passers-by are marked with green boxes, each with a small label. A security officer is watching the screen.

exercises.task: Give a talk about surveillance technology in public spaces.
content_points: describe the picture
explain the arguments for using such technology
discuss the risks for privacy and civil liberties
give your opinion on where limits should be set
follow_up_questions: Would you feel safer or more uncomfortable in a station like this?
What could happen if such technology made mistakes?
Should private companies be allowed to use facial recognition in shops?
Is the argument “I have nothing to hide” convincing here?
How might surveillance change people’s behaviour, for example at protests?

useful_phrases.label: Balancing values
phrases: There is a tension between … and …
Security should not come at the expense of …
The question is where to draw the line.

model_outline.heading: Describe
points: cameras, AI marking faces, control room

model_outline.heading: Arguments for
points: crime prevention, finding missing persons, security at large events

model_outline.heading: Opinion
points: strict limits: only for serious crimes, with court approval and transparency

exercises.title: lol, brb, 👍
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: A chat between two friends
stimulus.content:
A: omg did u see the vid 😂😂
B: ya lol. ngl kinda cringe tho
A: fr 💀 brb dinner
B: 👍

exercises.task: Give a talk about how digital communication is changing the way we write and speak.
content_points: describe the features of the language in the chat
discuss whether this is a threat to language or a natural development
consider how digital communication affects formal writing skills
follow_up_questions: Do you write differently to friends, parents and teachers? How?
Are emojis a kind of language?
Should schools allow abbreviations in informal writing tasks?
Can text messages be misunderstood more easily than speech? Why?
Which English slang expressions have entered German?

useful_phrases.label: Analysing language
phrases: Abbreviations such as … are used to …

model_outline.heading: Describe
points: abbreviations, slang, emojis, no capitals or punctuation

model_outline.heading: Threat or development?
points: linguists often see texting as a new register, not decline

model_outline.heading: Formal writing
points: but most people switch registers successfully

model_outline.heading: Conclusion
points: the key skill is choosing the right register for the situation

exercises.title: Talk at a school event
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Situation
stimulus.content: Your school is organising a “Media Literacy Day” for students aged 12–14. You have been asked to give a short talk to help them recognise false information online.

exercises.task: Give the talk to the younger students.
content_points: explain what misinformation and disinformation are, with examples
explain why false information spreads so easily
give practical tips for checking information
follow_up_questions: How did you adapt your language for a younger audience?
Which tip do you think is the most important, and why?
Why do people believe information that is obviously false?
Who should teach media literacy – parents, schools or platforms?
Have you ever believed or shared something that turned out to be false?

useful_phrases.label: Addressing an audience
phrases: Let me give you an example.
The most important thing to remember is …

model_outline.heading: Engaging opening
points: a question or example the audience knows

model_outline.heading: Tips and closing
points: stop, check the source, look for other reports, find the original

exercises.title: The price of fame
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: A famous singer is leaving a restaurant with a small child, trying to cover the child’s face with a jacket. A crowd of photographers is pushing forward, flashes going off. Several fans are filming with their phones.

exercises.task: Give a talk about the privacy of famous people.
content_points: describe the picture
discuss whether famous people have a right to privacy
consider the role of fans with smartphones, not only professional photographers
follow_up_questions: Should the children of celebrities be protected more strongly?
Is there a difference between politicians and entertainers when it comes to privacy?
Why are people so interested in celebrities’ private lives?
Would you like to be famous? Why (not)?
Do influencers give up their privacy voluntarily?

useful_phrases.label: Distinguishing
phrases: We need to distinguish between … and …
It is one thing to …, but quite another to …
Public interest is not the same as what interests the public.

model_outline.heading: Describe
points: singer protecting child, photographers and fans filming

model_outline.heading: Conclusion
points: famous people deserve privacy in private moments, especially children

exercises.title: Meeting up online
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: Split screen: on the left, a teenager in Austria wearing a headset is laughing in front of a computer. On the right, two other teenagers in different countries are playing the same online game and talking into their microphones. A chat window shows messages in English.

exercises.task: Give a talk about online gaming as a way of communicating.
content_points: describe the picture
discuss the social side of online gaming
talk about possible risks
say whether gaming can help people learn languages
follow_up_questions: Can friendships made through gaming be as strong as other friendships?
How should players deal with toxic behaviour in games?
Should parents limit gaming time? At what age?
Why is English so dominant in online gaming?
Is gaming taken seriously enough as a hobby?

model_outline.heading: Describe
points: players from different countries, headsets, English chat

model_outline.heading: Risks
points: toxic behaviour, contact with strangers, excessive time

model_outline.heading: Language learning
points: real communication in English, informal vocabulary

exercises.title: The AI news presenter
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Fictional headline (invented for this task)
stimulus.content: “Regional TV channel replaces evening news presenter with AI avatar – ‘Cheaper, faster, never sick’, says manager”

exercises.task: Give a talk about the use of artificial intelligence in journalism.
content_points: react to the headline
discuss how AI could help journalists
discuss the risks for quality, jobs and trust
say which tasks should remain in human hands
follow_up_questions: Would you trust news read by an AI avatar? Why (not)?
Should media outlets always say when AI was used to produce content?
Could AI make local journalism affordable again?
What happens to accountability when AI makes a mistake?
Which jobs in the media industry are most likely to change?

model_outline.heading: How AI helps
points: transcribing, translating, analysing data, routine reports

model_outline.heading: Risks
points: errors and invented facts, job losses, loss of trust

exercises.title: Politics in 30 seconds
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: A politician in a suit is standing in front of a phone on a small tripod, holding a coffee cup and making a funny face. A young assistant behind the phone is giving a thumbs-up. On a screen in the background, comments with heart emojis are scrolling past.

exercises.task: Give a talk about politicians using short-video platforms to reach young voters.
content_points: describe the picture
explain why politicians use such platforms
discuss the effects on political debate
give your opinion on whether this engages or manipulates young people
follow_up_questions: Have you seen political content on social media? What was it like?
Can complex political issues be explained in 30 seconds?
Should political advertising on social media be restricted?
Why do some young people feel ignored by politics?
Where should young voters get information before an election?

useful_phrases.label: Evaluating
phrases: Whether this is positive depends on …

model_outline.heading: Why
points: reach young people where they are

model_outline.heading: Effects
points: but more young people engage with politics

model_outline.heading: Opinion
points: engagement is good, but needs content and fact-checking

exercises.title: One star
exercises.instruction: Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Picture description
stimulus.content: The owner of a small family restaurant is sitting at an empty table, looking worried at a laptop. On the screen there is a review website showing several one-star reviews posted on the same day, all with very similar wording.

exercises.task: Give a talk about the power of online reviews.
content_points: describe and interpret the picture
explain why online reviews are so influential
discuss the problem of fake or unfair reviews
say how consumers can judge reviews critically
follow_up_questions: Do you read reviews before buying something or choosing a restaurant?
Should it be illegal to buy fake reviews?
Is it fair that one bad review can damage a small business?
Have you ever written a review? Why?
How can platforms make reviews more trustworthy?

useful_phrases.label: Speculating
phrases: This could be a case of …

model_outline.heading: Describe and interpret
points: worried owner, many similar one-star reviews – possibly fake or a coordinated attack

model_outline.heading: Why influential
points: social proof, trust in other customers

model_outline.heading: Critical reading
points: look for detail, patterns, dates, verified purchases
conclusion: useful but not the whole truth

exercises.title: Why press freedom matters
exercises.instruction: Extra challenge. Prepare a structured talk on the task below. Cover all the points.

stimulus.title: Statement for discussion
stimulus.content: “A democracy without a free press is like a house without windows: it may look solid from the outside, but nobody can see what is happening inside.” (statement written for this task)

exercises.task: Give a talk about the importance of press freedom.
content_points: interpret the statement
explain the role of journalism in a democracy, with an example
discuss current threats to press freedom
say what citizens can do to support independent journalism
follow_up_questions: Is press freedom also under threat in European democracies?
Should there be limits to press freedom, for example to protect privacy?
How do online harassment and lawsuits affect journalists?
Does social media strengthen or weaken press freedom?
Would you consider a career in journalism? Why (not)?

useful_phrases.label: Interpreting a metaphor
phrases: In this comparison, the windows stand for …

model_outline.heading: Interpret
points: windows = transparency; without them, abuse of power stays hidden

model_outline.heading: Threats
points: authoritarian pressure, SLAPPs, online harassment, economic decline of local media

model_outline.heading: Citizens
points: pay for quality journalism, share responsibly, support public service media with independence safeguards
